CHAPTER 7

Geometric and physical applications

Integral applications share one method: determine how a small element contributes, then accumulate over an interval. Area, volume, length, mass, and work use different elements.

  1. Set up area and volume integrals
  2. Derive arc length and average value
  3. Distinguish displacement, distance, work, and mass

SECTION 7.1

Area between curves

How tall is each strip?

The idea

Add the areas of thin strips. Vertical strips use top minus bottom; horizontal strips use right minus left.

Intuition

Between y=xy = xy=x and y=x2y = x^{2}y=x2 on [0,1][0,1][0,1], each vertical height is x−x2x - x^{2}x−x2. The area is ∫01(x−x2)dx=16\int _{0}^{1} (x - x^{2}) \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{6}∫01​(x−x2)dx=61​.

Another explanation

Find the strip height first, then accumulate its area. Use top minus bottom; if the curves exchange places, reverse the order by splitting the interval.

Quick check

How do you find area when two curves cross inside the interval?

  1. Always subtract the second curve from the first
  2. Split at intersections and use top minus bottom on each piece
  3. Use only the height difference at the intersection
Answer & explanation

B. Area cannot cancel by sign. Find intersections and curve order, then integrate piecewise, or integrate the absolute height difference.

What comes first?

Find intersections, then determine which curve is above on each piece. Split wherever the order changes to prevent cancellation.

When are horizontal strips easier?

Use ∫(right−left) dy\int(\text{right}-\text{left})\,\mathrm{d}y∫(right−left)dy when the curves are easily written as x=g(y)x = g (y)x=g(y) or this direction needs fewer pieces. Identify each strip's left and right boundaries first.

Can you use absolute values directly?

Write ∫∣f−g∣dx\int |f - g| \mathrm{d}x∫∣f−g∣dx. To evaluate it, usually split at intersections and remove the absolute values on each piece. Area is nonnegative, unlike signed accumulation.

Definition and conditions

When fff lies above ggg, accumulate vertical strips to find the area.

A=∫ab[f(x)−g(x)]dxA=\int_a^b[f(x)-g(x)]dxA=∫ab​[f(x)−g(x)]dx
  1. Assume f≥gf \ge gf≥g and both functions are integrable on the interval. Split where their order changes.

Derivation

On [0,1][0,1][0,1], x≥x2x \ge x^{2}x≥x2, so the height is x−x2x - x^{2}x−x2.

dA=(x−x2)dxdA=(x-x^2)dxdA=(x−x2)dx

Integrate and substitute the endpoints.

A=[x22−x33]01A=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1A=[2x2​−3x3​]01​

The result is a nonnegative area.

A=16A=\frac16A=61​

Worked examples

  2. Integrating x−x2x - x^{2}x−x2 gives 12−13\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}21​−31​.

Example 2: When the order changes

  2. Each triangle has area 1.

The total area is 2. Integrating 2x2 x2x throughout would incorrectly cancel the pieces.

Common mistakes

Using the same subtraction order without checking intersections.

Split where top and bottom exchange, or use absolute values.

Calling a negative integral a geometric area.

First make sure every strip height is nonnegative.

SECTION 7.2

Volumes by cross sections: disks, washers, and more

Accumulate cross-sectional area

The idea

Slice a solid along one direction. Its volume is the integral of cross-sectional area along that direction. Solids of revolution often have disk or washer cross sections.

Intuition

Rotating around the xxx-axis turns height into radius. A solid disk has area πR2\pi R^{2}πR2; a hole removes πr2\pi r^{2}πr2. Multiply by slice thickness.

Another explanation

A slice contributes its cross-sectional area times thickness. Use a disk area, a difference of disk areas, or the area formula for the actual shape.

Quick check

What is the area of a washer with outer radius 2 and inner radius 1?

  1. π\piπ
  2. 3π3 \pi3π
  3. 9π9 \pi9π
Answer & explanation

B. Subtract the inner disk from the outer: π⋅22−π⋅12=3π\pi \cdot 2^{2} - \pi \cdot 1^{2} = 3 \piπ⋅22−π⋅12=3π. Subtracting radii before squaring loses the geometry.

Where do you measure the radius?

From the axis to the boundary. Around y=ky = ky=k, the radius is ∣y−k∣|y - k|∣y−k∣. The outer radius reaches the boundary farther from the axis, which need not be the higher curve.

Why not π(R−r)2\pi (R - r)^{2}π(R−r)2?

A washer is a large disk minus a small disk, giving π(R2−r2)\pi (R^{2} - r^{2})π(R2−r2). Horizontal axes often use dx\mathrm{d}xdx; vertical axes often use dy\mathrm{d}ydy. Slices must be perpendicular to the axis.

When are shells easier?

If washers require inverse functions or many pieces, try shells. If the axis passes through the region, check the actual swept solid; blindly subtracting top and bottom can fail.

Can you use cross sections without rotation?

Yes. If the area perpendicular to the xxx direction is A(x)A(x)A(x), then V=∫abA(x) dxV=\int_a^b A(x)\,\mathrm{d}xV=∫ab​A(x)dx. Disks are the special case A=πR2A=\pi R^2A=πR2. Squares use side length squared; triangles use half base times height. Determine the shape before writing its area.

Definition and conditions

For outer radius RRR and inner radius rrr with R≥r≥0R\ge r\ge0R≥r≥0:

V=π∫ab[R(x)2−r(x)2]dxV=\pi\int_a^b\left[R(x)^2-r(x)^2\right]dxV=π∫ab​[R(x)2−r(x)2]dx
  1. Assume a<ba < ba<b, with RRR and rrr continuous on [a,b][a , b][a,b] and R≥r≥0R \ge r \ge 0R≥r≥0.
  2. Slices are perpendicular to the axis and radii are distances from it. A disk has r=0r = 0r=0.
  3. More generally, if A(x)A(x)A(x) is the solid's actual nonnegative continuous cross-sectional area, then V=∫abA(x) dxV=\int_a^b A(x)\,\mathrm{d}xV=∫ab​A(x)dx, whether or not the solid is formed by rotation.

Derivation

Rotate the region bounded by y=xy = \sqrt{x}y=x​, the xxx-axis, and x=1x = 1x=1 about the xxx-axis.

R(x)=x,A(x)=πxR(x)=\sqrt x,\qquad A(x)=\pi xR(x)=x​,A(x)=πx

Accumulate thin disks along xxx.

V=π∫01x dxV=\pi\int_0^1x\,dxV=π∫01​xdx

Use the endpoint values to evaluate the volume.

V=π2V=\frac\pi2V=2π​

A radius is a distance from the axis, not necessarily a coordinate value.

Use the actual shape's area: circle area for a disk, side squared for a square. Integration supplies the thickness.

SECTION 7.3

Volumes by cylindrical shells

How far does a strip travel?

The idea

A strip parallel to the rotation axis sweeps out a thin cylindrical shell. Its volume is approximately circumference×height×thickness\text{circumference}\times\text{height}\times\text{thickness}circumference×height×thickness.

Intuition

Unroll a thin shell: it has length 2πr2 \pi r2πr, height hhh, and thickness dr\mathrm{d}rdr. Its contribution is approximately 2πrh dr2\pi rh\,\mathrm{d}r2πrhdr.

Another explanation

A strip parallel to the rotation axis forms a thin shell. Multiply circumference, height, and thickness; do not replace circumference with disk area.

Quick check

Rotate 0≤y≤x20 \le y \le x^{2}0≤y≤x2, 0≤x≤10 \le x \le 10≤x≤1 about the yyy-axis. What is the height of a shell of radius xxx?

  1. xxx
  2. x2x^{2}x2
  3. 1−x21 - x^{2}1−x2
Answer & explanation

B. The strip runs from y=0y = 0y=0 to y=x2y = x^{2}y=x2, so its height is x2x^{2}x2. Its volume is approximately 2πx⋅x2⋅dx2 \pi x \cdot x^{2} \cdot \mathrm{d}x2πx⋅x2⋅dx.

How do you find radius and height?

For a vertical strip rotating about the yyy-axis with nonnegative horizontal coordinate, r=xr = xr=x and hhh is top minus bottom. Around x=kx = kx=k, r=∣x−k∣r = |x - k|r=∣x−k∣. Each shell must represent a distinct radius to avoid double counting.

Why can the thin-shell approximation be integrated?

An exact shell has volume π[(r+Δr)2−r2]h\pi [(r + \Delta r)^{2} - r^{2}] hπ[(r+Δr)2−r2]h. Expanding gives 2πrhΔr+πhΔr22 \pi r h \Delta r + \pi h \Delta r^{2}2πrhΔr+πhΔr2. Under refinement, the total second-order error tends to zero, leaving the integral.

How can you check the answer?

Washers for the same region must give the same volume. If the axis passes through the region, shells from opposite sides may overlap. Choose a description without repeated coverage.

Definition and conditions

The cylindrical shell volume formula.

V=2π∫abr(x)h(x)dxV=2\pi\int_a^b r(x)h(x)dxV=2π∫ab​r(x)h(x)dx
  1. Assume a<ba < ba<b, with continuous nonnegative radius rrr and height hhh on [a,b][a , b][a,b]. Shells must not overlap in coverage.
  2. Slices are parallel to the axis; xxx measures perpendicular distance so dx\mathrm{d}xdx is radial thickness. For example, about the yyy-axis with x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, r=xr = xr=x.

Derivation

Rotate 0≤x≤10 \le x \le 10≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x20 \le y \le x^{2}0≤y≤x2 about the yyy-axis.

r=x,h=x2r=x,\qquad h=x^2r=x,h=x2

A thin shell contributes 2πx3dx2 \pi x^{3} \mathrm{d}x2πx3dx.

V=2π∫01x3dxV=2\pi\int_0^1x^3dxV=2π∫01​x3dx

Integration gives π2\frac{\pi }{2}2π​.

V=π2V=\frac\pi2V=2π​

SECTION 7.4

Arc length and surface area of revolution

Add short lengths, not heights

The idea

Arc length adds the Pythagorean lengths of small segments. Surface area of revolution adds the narrow bands swept out by those segments.

Intuition

A small segment moves horizontally by dx\mathrm{d}xdx and vertically by about f′dxf' \mathrm{d}xf′dx, giving length 1+f′2dx\sqrt{1 + {f'}^{2}} \mathrm{d}x1+f′2​dx. Following the curve is longer than measuring its horizontal span.

Another explanation

Length includes both horizontal and vertical change. Rotation sweeps this slant length into a band, so horizontal width alone is insufficient.

Quick check

Which length multiplies circumference in a narrow band of a surface of revolution?

  1. Horizontal width dx\mathrm{d}xdx
  2. Slant length ds=1+f′(x)2dx\mathrm{d}s = \sqrt{1 + f' (x)^{2}} \mathrm{d}xds=1+f′(x)2​dx
  3. Function height f(x)f (x)f(x)
Answer & explanation

B. The band follows the curve, so its width is arc length ds\mathrm{d}sds. Using only dx\mathrm{d}xdx omits the slant. This calculates lateral area only.

How do you calculate arc length?

For continuously differentiable fff on [a,b][a , b][a,b], integrate 1+f′2\sqrt{1 + {f'}^{2}}1+f′2​. Squaring the slope makes descending sections contribute positive length too. Arc length generally differs from the straight distance between endpoints.

What if you cannot integrate the formula?

Use numerical methods or write x=g(y)x = g (y)x=g(y) and integrate with respect to yyy. The absence of an elementary antiderivative does not make the length undefined.

Why multiply by circumference for surface area?

When f≥0f \ge 0f≥0 rotates about the xxx-axis, a segment ds\mathrm{d}sds sweeps a band with circumference 2πf2 \pi f2πf and area approximately 2πfds2 \pi f \mathrm{d}s2πfds. The integral counts the lateral surface only; add end caps separately. A different axis changes the radius.

Definition and conditions

Arc length and lateral surface area about the xxx-axis.

L=∫ab1+[f′(x)]2 dx,S=2π∫abf(x)1+[f′(x)]2 dxL=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+[f\prime(x)]^2}\,dx,\qquad S=2\pi\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+[f\prime(x)]^2}\,dxL=∫ab​1+[f′(x)]2​dx,S=2π∫ab​f(x)1+[f′(x)]2​dx
  1. Assume fff is continuously differentiable on [a,b][a , b][a,b]. The surface formula here requires f≥0f \ge 0f≥0 and excludes end caps.

Derivation

A horizontal change Δx\Delta xΔx and vertical change Δy\Delta yΔy form a right triangle.

Δs=(Δx)2+(Δy)2\Delta s=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}Δs=(Δx)2+(Δy)2​

Divide out the horizontal scale; the segment slope tends to f′f'f′.

ds=1+(f′)2 dxds=\sqrt{1+(f\prime)^2}\,dxds=1+(f′)2​dx

Adding the segment lengths gives the arc length integral.

L=∫abdsL=\int_a^b dsL=∫ab​ds

3. Inspect a rotated band

Common mistakes

That gives signed accumulation, usually interpreted as area. Arc length depends on slope.

Treating lateral surface area as total area of a closed solid.

Add the appropriate end caps when total surface area is requested.

SECTION 7.5

Displacement, work, mass, and averages

Accumulate local contributions

The idea

Write a small contribution before integrating: velocity×time\text{velocity}\times\text{time}velocity×time gives displacement, force×displacement\text{force}\times\text{displacement}force×displacement gives work, and linear density×length\text{linear density}\times\text{length}linear density×length gives mass.

Intuition

Units help identify the right factors: ms×s=m\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}sm​×s=m, N×m=J\mathrm{N}\times\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{J}N×m=J, and kgm×m=kg\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}}\times\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{kg}mkg​×m=kg.

Another explanation

Match each contribution with its units before integrating. Negative velocity tracks direction, weight times lift distance gives work, and density times volume gives mass.

Quick check

If velocity v(t)v (t)v(t) has both signs, what should you integrate for total distance?

  1. v(t)v (t)v(t)
  2. ∣v(t)∣|v (t)|∣v(t)∣
  3. v′(t)v' (t)v′(t)
Answer & explanation

B. Displacement integrates signed v(t)v (t)v(t); distance integrates speed ∣v(t)∣|v (t)|∣v(t)∣. Backtracking cancels displacement but never distance.

How do displacement and distance differ?

Displacement is ∫vdt\int v \mathrm{d}t∫vdt; distance is ∫∣v∣dt\int |v| \mathrm{d}t∫∣v∣dt. Split where velocity changes sign. Add initial position to recover position. Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time.

How do you calculate variable-force work?

The force component along motion contributes dW=F(x)dx\mathrm{d}W = F (x) \mathrm{d}xdW=F(x)dx. Stretching a spring requires external force kxk xkx, giving work ∫kx dx\int kx\,\mathrm{d}x∫kxdx. The spring's restoring force points the other way.

How do you find mass and center of mass?

Linear density λ\lambdaλ gives mass m=∫λdxm = \int \lambda \mathrm{d}xm=∫λdx. The first moment is M=∫xλdxM = \int x \lambda \mathrm{d}xM=∫xλdx, so the center of mass is Mm\frac{M}{m}mM​ for m>0m > 0m>0. Physical models such as fluid pressure also need assumptions about density and depth.

Why does pumping water need varying lift distances?

With tank bottom y=0y=0y=0 and outlet height HHH, a layer at height yyy has volume A(y) dyA(y)\,\mathrm{d}yA(y)dy and must rise H−yH-yH−y. Thus W=∫ρgA(y)(H−y) dyW=\int\rho gA(y)(H-y)\,\mathrm{d}yW=∫ρgA(y)(H−y)dy over the actual water layers. Assume constant density ρ\rhoρ and gravity ggg, negligible losses, and negligible exit speed.

How does water pressure accumulate into force?

Measure depth hhh downward from the surface. Gauge pressure is p=ρghp=\rho ghp=ρgh. A strip of width w(h)w(h)w(h) and height dh\mathrm{d}hdh receives force ρghw(h) dh\rho ghw(h)\,\mathrm{d}hρghw(h)dh. Integrate over depth to find the resultant on one side of a vertical plate. If both sides are pressurized, use their pressure difference.

Definition and conditions

Multiply each local contribution by the appropriate differential.

Δs=∫v(t)dt,W=∫F(x)dx,m=∫λ(x)dx,xˉ=∫xλ(x)dxm\Delta s=\int v(t)dt,\quad W=\int F(x)dx,\quad m=\int\lambda(x)dx,\quad\bar x=\frac{\int x\lambda(x)dx}{m}Δs=∫v(t)dt,W=∫F(x)dx,m=∫λ(x)dx,xˉ=m∫xλ(x)dx​
  1. Bounds must match the time or position interval. Density is nonnegative and center of mass requires positive total mass. Use the force component along displacement.

Derivation

For v(t)=t−1v (t) = t - 1v(t)=t−1 on 0≤t≤30 \le t \le 30≤t≤3, first locate the change of direction.

v(t)=0⇒t=1v(t)=0\Rightarrow t=1v(t)=0⇒t=1

Signed accumulation gives displacement.

Δs=∫03(t−1)dt=32\Delta s=\int_0^3(t-1)dt=\frac32Δs=∫03​(t−1)dt=23​

For distance, reverse the first piece's sign to obtain a larger total length.

D=−∫01(t−1)dt+∫13(t−1)dt=52D=-\int_0^1(t-1)dt+\int_1^3(t-1)dt=\frac52D=−∫01​(t−1)dt+∫13​(t−1)dt=25​

Common mistakes

Calling the integral of velocity total distance.

Negative velocity cancels positive velocity. Distance integrates absolute velocity.

Pairing the integrand with the wrong variable or units.

Force multiplies position change; flow rate multiplies time change. Check dimensions first.

Glossary

Domain
The set of allowed inputs.
Composition
The output of one function becomes the input to another.
Inverse function
A function that reverses a one-to-one input–output relation.
Radian
Arc length divided by radius.
Limit
The value approached by outputs as inputs approach a target.
Indeterminate form
A form such as 00\frac{0}{0}00​ that does not by itself determine a limit.
Continuity
The function value exists and equals the nearby limit.
Asymptote
A line describing a graph's limiting behavior near a boundary or far away.
Difference quotient
The average rate of change between two inputs.
Derivative
The finite limit of a difference quotient as the input separation tends to zero.
Chain rule
Multiply the rates of change through the layers of a composition.
Critical point
A point in the domain where the derivative is zero or undefined.
Inflection point
A point on a continuous curve where concavity changes.
Linearization
A local first-order approximation built from a tangent.
Riemann sum
A sum of sample heights times subinterval widths.
Antiderivative
A function whose derivative is the given function.
Definite integral
The signed limit of increasingly fine accumulated contributions.
Substitution
A change of integration variable based on the chain rule in reverse.
Arc length
The accumulated Pythagorean lengths of short curve segments.
Center of mass
The mass-weighted average position.
Integral mean value theorem
A continuous function on a closed interval of positive length attains its average value there.
Volume by cross sections
Accumulate cross-sectional area along a slicing direction; rotation is not required.
Gauge pressure
Pressure relative to surrounding atmospheric pressure; in a stationary fluid it increases with depth.

Proof supplements and scope

Proof supplement: basic trigonometric limits

On the unit circle, for 0<h<π20 < h < \frac{\pi }{2}0<h<2π​, the inscribed triangle, sector, and circumscribed triangle have increasing areas, giving sin⁡h<h<tan⁡h\sin h < h < \tan hsinh<h<tanh. Divide by sin⁡h\sin hsinh and rearrange to obtain cos⁡h<sin⁡hh<1\cos h < \frac{\sin h}{h} < 1cosh<hsinh​<1. Since cos⁡h→1\cos h \to 1cosh→1, squeezing gives right limit 1. The identity sin⁡(−h)−h=sin⁡hh\frac{\sin (- h)}{- h} = \frac{\sin h}{h}−hsin(−h)​=hsinh​ gives the same left limit. Rationalizing cos⁡h−1h\frac{\cos h - 1}{h}hcosh−1​ gives −[sin⁡hh][sin⁡h1+cos⁡h]- [\frac{\sin h}{h}] [\frac{\sin h}{1 + \cos h}]−[hsinh​][1+coshsinh​], whose limit is 0.

Proof supplement: Cauchy's mean value theorem

Suppose f,gf , gf,g are continuous on [a,b][a , b][a,b] and differentiable inside. Define H(x)=[f(b)−f(a)][g(x)−g(a)]−[g(b)−g(a)][f(x)−f(a)]H (x) = [f (b) - f (a)] [g (x) - g (a)] - [g (b) - g (a)] [f (x) - f (a)]H(x)=[f(b)−f(a)][g(x)−g(a)]−[g(b)−g(a)][f(x)−f(a)]. Both endpoint values of HHH are zero. Rolle's theorem gives H′(c)=0H' (c) = 0H′(c)=0, producing the cross-product identity. If g′g'g′ is nowhere zero inside, the mean value theorem also gives g(b)≠g(a)g (b) \ne g (a)g(b)=g(a), allowing division to equate the ratio of increments with a ratio of derivatives.

Proof supplement: the sum of squares

Start with (i+1)3−i3=3i2+3i+1(i + 1)^{3} - i^{3} = 3 i^{2} + 3 i + 1(i+1)3−i3=3i2+3i+1 and sum over i=1,…,ni = 1 , … , ni=1,…,n. The left side telescopes. Use ∑i=n(n+1)2\sum i = \frac{n (n + 1)}{2}∑i=2n(n+1)​ and rearrange to obtain ∑i2=n(n+1)(2n+1)6\sum i^{2} = \frac{n (n + 1) (2 n + 1)}{6}∑i2=6n(n+1)(2n+1)​. This turns the right Riemann sum for x2x^{2}x2 into an explicit finite expression.

Scope and the next volumes

This book covers single-variable Calculus I. Systematic integration by parts, partial fractions, trigonometric substitution, improper integrals, sequences, and Taylor series belong to Calculus II. Partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector calculus belong to Calculus III. Those volumes are complete books rather than placeholder chapters here.

Sources and provenance

AI-authored; not individually human-reviewed. Sources informed scope, mathematical conditions, and teaching design. Checks are not formal proofs.

OpenStax · Calculus Volume 1

Used to check scope and theorem hypotheses. Explanations, worked solutions, and interactive diagrams were independently written; source prose and images were not copied.

Active Calculus · Single Variable, Second Edition

Informed the organization around problems and activities. Source prose, activities, and questions were not copied.

IES · Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning

Informed the use of linked text and diagrams, interleaved examples and exercises, and spaced review. This does not establish the effectiveness of this textbook.

PhET · Research and Simulation Design

Informed the design of limited controls, immediate feedback, and multiple representations. Three-dimensional models and diagrams were independently implemented.

3Blue1Brown · Essence of Calculus

Informed geometric explanations connecting limits, derivatives, and integrals. Video, images, and wording were not copied.

MIT OCW · 18.01SC Syllabus

Used as a reference for course goals and self-study organization. The MIT course also covers material beyond this volume.

Agarwal, Nunes & Blunt · Retrieval Practice (2021)

Research reference for retrieval and feedback. The mathematics sample is limited; multiple-choice checks are not treated as complete retrieval practice.

CMU Eberly Center · Choosing an Appropriate Approach

Informed explanations of method selection and mixed exercises that check transfer.
